label: A mathematical story from 1950
title: Messages learn to repair themselves
explanation: Richard Hamming published a systematic method for adding carefully placed check bits to a binary message. A receiver can use the pattern of failed checks to locate and correct a single wrong bit, rather than merely noticing that something went wrong.
whyItMatters: Hamming codes helped establish coding theory and still illustrate how mathematical structure makes digital communication reliable.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1951
title: A layered tool connects shapes
explanation: Jean-Pierre Serre used spectral sequences to relate three parts of a mathematical construction called a fibration: its base, its fibre and its total space. The method works like a sequence of increasingly accurate pages that reveal otherwise hidden information about a shape.
whyItMatters: This connected homology and homotopy and made spectral sequences a central calculating tool in modern topology.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1952
title: Dense sets must contain arithmetic patterns
explanation: Klaus Roth proved that any set containing a positive proportion of the whole numbers must contain three numbers in arithmetic progression, such as 5, 11 and 17. A set can avoid every such three-term pattern only by becoming thinner and thinner among the integers.
whyItMatters: Roth's theorem launched powerful methods for finding unavoidable patterns inside apparently irregular sets of numbers.
sourceTitle: Fields Medals 1958 - International Mathematical Union

label: A mathematical story from 1953
title: Random steps become a scientific calculator
people: Nicholas Metropolis, Arianna Rosenbluth, Marshall Rosenbluth, Augusta Teller and Edward Teller
explanation: A five-person team introduced the Metropolis algorithm, which samples likely states of a complicated system by taking controlled random steps. Instead of checking every possibility, the method spends more time in the regions that matter most and uses those samples to estimate an answer.
whyItMatters: This became a foundation of Markov chain Monte Carlo, now used across statistics, physics, biology and machine learning.
sourceTitle: Equation of State Calculations by Fast Computing Machines - Journal of Chemical Physics

label: A mathematical story from 1954
title: Order survives small disturbances
explanation: Andrey Kolmogorov presented the central idea that many regular motions in an ideal dynamical system survive when the system is changed slightly. Arnold and Moser later completed and extended the theory now called KAM theory.
whyItMatters: KAM theory explains why some planetary and mechanical motions can remain stable even when real systems are not perfectly ideal.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1955
title: Elliptic curves are linked to modular forms
people: Yutaka Taniyama, with later development by Goro Shimura
explanation: Yutaka Taniyama proposed that elliptic curves over the rational numbers should correspond to highly symmetric objects called modular forms. The idea was surprising because the two families are defined in very different ways, and its precise form was refined later.
whyItMatters: This bridge became the modularity theorem and supplied the decisive route to Fermat's Last Theorem decades later.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1956
title: A sphere can be smooth in more than one way
explanation: John Milnor showed that a seven-dimensional sphere can carry different smooth structures: versions that are topologically the same but cannot be smoothly reshaped into one another. These unexpected objects became known as exotic spheres.
whyItMatters: The discovery opened differential topology and revealed that 'same shape' can have different meanings in topology and calculus.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1957
title: Functions of many variables reduce to simpler pieces
explanation: Kolmogorov and Arnold showed that every continuous function of several variables can be assembled from continuous functions of fewer variables together with addition. Their work resolved the continuous form of Hilbert's thirteenth problem, although it did not settle versions with stricter conditions such as algebraic functions.
whyItMatters: The theorem revealed that extremely complicated multivariable behaviour can be encoded using surprisingly simple building blocks.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1958
title: Cobordism classifies shapes by their boundaries
explanation: René Thom received a Fields Medal for developing cobordism, which groups spaces together when their combined boundary forms a higher-dimensional space. This turned a visual idea about boundaries into an algebraic way to classify manifolds.
whyItMatters: Cobordism became a model for connecting geometry, topology and algebra and led to important generalized cohomology theories.
sourceTitle: Fields Medals 1958 - International Mathematical Union

label: A mathematical story from 1959
title: Some group questions have no universal algorithm
explanation: William Boone completed a proof that there is no algorithm which always decides whether two written expressions describe the same element of an arbitrary finitely presented group. The problem is easy for some groups, but impossible to solve uniformly for all of them.
whyItMatters: The result showed that the limits of computation occur inside abstract algebra, not only in specially designed logic puzzles.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1950-1960 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1960
title: New infinite families of simple groups appear
explanation: Michio Suzuki discovered previously unknown infinite families of finite simple groups, mathematical objects that cannot be broken into smaller normal pieces. These Suzuki groups joined the basic families from which all finite groups are ultimately assembled.
whyItMatters: The discovery expanded the periodic table of finite symmetry and became essential to the later classification of finite simple groups.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1961
title: The Poincare conjecture yields in higher dimensions
explanation: Stephen Smale proved the Poincare conjecture for manifolds of dimension five and higher using a powerful reshaping tool called the h-cobordism theorem. The familiar three-dimensional case remained open for more than four further decades.
whyItMatters: The proof transformed high-dimensional topology and showed that extra dimensions can sometimes make a geometric problem easier rather than harder.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1962
title: Lie algebras gain a defining reference
explanation: Nathan Jacobson published his influential book Lie Algebras, organizing a theory that describes continuous symmetries through algebraic rules. Lie algebras turn small, local motions near an identity into equations that are often easier to study.
whyItMatters: The framework is central to modern geometry and algebra and also provides the mathematical language for many symmetries in physics.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1963
title: The continuum hypothesis is independent
explanation: Paul Cohen invented forcing and used it to prove that the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice cannot be derived from the usual Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms, assuming those axioms are consistent. Together with Gödel's earlier work, this showed the continuum hypothesis can be neither proved nor disproved from the standard axioms.
whyItMatters: The result changed set theory by showing that some precise mathematical questions depend on which consistent axioms mathematicians choose.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1964
title: Algebraic singularities can be resolved
explanation: Heisuke Hironaka proved that algebraic varieties over fields of characteristic zero can have their singular points resolved into smooth geometry through a controlled sequence of modifications. In effect, a shape with pinches or crossings can be replaced by a closely related smooth one.
whyItMatters: Resolution of singularities became a fundamental tool in algebraic geometry, although the general positive-characteristic case remains open.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1965
title: The fast Fourier transform accelerates calculation
explanation: Cooley and Tukey published an efficient algorithm for computing a discrete Fourier transform by repeatedly splitting one large problem into smaller ones. The core idea had earlier ancestors, but their paper made the fast Fourier transform practical for digital computers.
whyItMatters: The FFT made signal processing, image compression, spectral analysis and many scientific simulations dramatically faster.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1966
title: A computer overturns Euler's powers conjecture
explanation: Lander and Parkin found four fifth powers whose sum is another fifth power, contradicting a conjecture Euler had made about how many powers were required. A computer search produced the explicit equality rather than a general theoretical argument.
whyItMatters: The counterexample showed how computation can test vast numerical territories and decisively correct long-accepted mathematical guesses.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1967
title: K-theory turns geometry into algebra
explanation: Michael Atiyah published a major account of topological K-theory, which studies a space by organizing the vector bundles that can sit over it. Addition and subtraction of these bundles create algebraic objects that record subtle geometric information.
whyItMatters: K-theory became a bridge among topology, algebra, geometry and the index theory of differential equations.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1968
title: Bounded repetition can still create infinite groups
explanation: Novikov and Adian proved that certain groups can be infinite even when every element returns to the identity after a fixed number of repetitions. Their result answered a major form of the Burnside problem for sufficiently large odd exponents.
whyItMatters: It revealed that simple local repetition rules do not force an algebraic system to have only finitely many possible states.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1969
title: Three exceptional symmetry groups emerge
explanation: John Conway published the construction of three new sporadic simple groups from symmetries of the 24-dimensional Leech lattice. Sporadic means they are exceptional objects rather than members of an infinite family.
whyItMatters: The Conway groups linked geometry, lattices and finite symmetry and helped reveal the much larger Monster group soon afterward.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1960-1970 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1970
title: Hilbert's tenth problem has no general algorithm
people: Yuri Matiyasevich, building on Martin Davis, Hilary Putnam and Julia Robinson
explanation: Yuri Matiyasevich completed the proof that no algorithm can always decide whether a polynomial equation with integer coefficients has an integer solution. His work supplied the missing link in results developed by Davis, Putnam and Robinson.
whyItMatters: The theorem places an exact limit on computation using equations that can be written with familiar whole-number arithmetic.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1971
title: The P versus NP question takes shape
explanation: Stephen Cook proved that Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete: every problem whose proposed answers can be checked quickly can be efficiently translated into it. This made the P versus NP problem a precise central question about whether quickly checkable problems are also quickly solvable.
whyItMatters: NP-completeness gives computer science a map of thousands of difficult problems and explains why a fast solution to one could transform them all.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1972
title: Higher algebraic K-theory is created
explanation: Daniel Quillen introduced higher algebraic K-theory, extending earlier ideas so that rings and other algebraic objects have an entire sequence of K-groups. His constructions used topology to package increasingly subtle algebraic information.
whyItMatters: The theory provided new tools for algebra and number theory and later became part of deep connections among geometry, topology and arithmetic.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1973
title: The Weil conjectures are completed
explanation: Pierre Deligne completed a proof of the final and deepest Weil conjecture, controlling the sizes of numbers that arise when algebraic equations are counted over finite fields. His proof built on the cohomology theory developed by Grothendieck and others and was published the following year.
whyItMatters: The result connected geometry, topology and number theory and supplied powerful estimates used throughout modern arithmetic geometry.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1974
title: Moduli spaces organize families of shapes
explanation: David Mumford received a Fields Medal for work that gave algebraic geometers rigorous ways to build moduli spaces, spaces whose points represent other geometric objects. His geometric invariant theory explains when different-looking descriptions should count as the same object.
whyItMatters: Moduli spaces let mathematicians study an entire family of curves or shapes as one geometric object instead of one example at a time.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1975
title: A universal number appears on the route to chaos
explanation: Mitchell Feigenbaum discovered that many very different systems approach chaos through period doubling at the same numerical rate, about 4.669. This constant appears even when the systems use different formulas, provided they share the right broad shape.
whyItMatters: Feigenbaum universality showed that apparently unrelated nonlinear systems can follow the same mathematical road from order to chaos.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1976
title: Four colours are enough
explanation: Appel and Haken proved that every flat map can be coloured with at most four colours so that neighbouring regions differ. Their proof reduced the question to many unavoidable configurations and used extensive computer calculations to check them.
whyItMatters: It settled a famous problem and forced mathematicians to think carefully about how computer-assisted proofs can be checked and trusted.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1977
title: Public keys make secret messages practical
people: Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman
explanation: Rivest, Shamir and Adleman introduced RSA, a public-key system in which anyone can use a published key to encrypt a message but only the holder of a private key can efficiently decrypt it. Its arithmetic relies on modular exponentiation and the difficulty of factoring large composite numbers.
whyItMatters: RSA turned number theory into a practical foundation for secure digital communication and electronic signatures.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1978
title: Positive curvature identifies projective space
explanation: Shigefumi Mori proved the Hartshorne conjecture that a smooth complete algebraic variety with an ample tangent bundle must be projective space. Roughly, a strong algebraic version of positive curvature forces the entire space to have the standard projective form.
whyItMatters: The proof was an early success of methods that grew into Mori theory, a major program for classifying algebraic varieties.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1979
title: Integration enters a noncommutative world
explanation: Alain Connes published foundational work on integrating in settings where multiplication may depend on order, so ab need not equal ba. He treated operator algebras as if they were coordinate systems for unusual geometric spaces.
whyItMatters: This helped launch noncommutative geometry, which links analysis, geometry, number theory and mathematical physics.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1970-1980 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1980
title: Finite simple groups receive a classification
people: A large international community of mathematicians
explanation: By 1980 mathematicians announced that the classification of finite simple groups was essentially complete: every such group belongs to an infinite family or is one of 26 sporadic exceptions. The proof was spread across thousands of pages and later required repairs, simplifications and a continuing effort to produce a more unified account.
whyItMatters: Finite simple groups are the basic building blocks of finite symmetry, so their classification is often compared with a periodic table.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1981
title: The ellipsoid method reaches combinatorial problems
people: Martin Grötschel, László Lovász and Alexander Schrijver
explanation: Grötschel, Lovász and Schrijver showed that the ellipsoid method could solve broad families of combinatorial optimization problems in polynomial time, at least in theory. Their work connected the geometry of convex bodies with questions about graphs, matchings and submodular functions.
whyItMatters: It established deep equivalences between optimization and separation and changed how mathematicians classify the difficulty of discrete problems.
sourceTitle: The Ellipsoid Method and Its Consequences in Combinatorial Optimization - CWI

label: A mathematical story from 1982
title: Four-dimensional spaces are classified topologically
explanation: Michael Freedman proved a far-reaching classification theorem for simply connected topological four-manifolds and settled the four-dimensional topological Poincare conjecture. Four dimensions behave unusually: a space can be topologically standard while its smooth structure is far more complicated.
whyItMatters: The work opened a new understanding of dimension four and set the stage for striking contrasts between topology and smooth geometry.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1983
title: The Mordell conjecture is proved
explanation: Gerd Faltings proved that a curve of genus greater than one defined over the rational numbers has only finitely many rational points. The theorem does not automatically list those points, but it proves there cannot be infinitely many of them.
whyItMatters: The result settled a major conjecture and transformed the study of equations whose solutions are required to be rational numbers.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1984
title: A new polynomial distinguishes knots
explanation: Vaughan Jones discovered a polynomial that can be calculated from a knot diagram but stays unchanged when the diagram is moved without cutting the knot. The Jones polynomial could distinguish knots that earlier tools could not tell apart.
whyItMatters: The invariant created unexpected links among knot theory, operator algebras, statistical mechanics and quantum physics.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1985
title: The universal quantum computer is defined
explanation: David Deutsch described a mathematical model of a universal quantum computer, extending Turing's model so information follows the rules of quantum mechanics. His paper showed how quantum parallelism could give computation properties unavailable to a purely classical restriction.
whyItMatters: The model supplied a theoretical foundation for quantum algorithms and for the modern study of quantum computational complexity.
field: Theoretical computer science and mathematical physics
sourceTitle: Quantum Theory, the Church-Turing Principle and the Universal Quantum Computer - Royal Society

label: A mathematical story from 1986
title: The Oppenheim conjecture is proved
explanation: Grigory Margulis proved that an indefinite irrational quadratic form in at least three variables takes values arbitrarily close to zero at nonzero integer points. His proof translated a number-theory problem into the motion of points on a homogeneous space.
whyItMatters: The solution pioneered interactions between dynamics, Lie groups and number theory that now form a major research area.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1987
title: A Lie-algebra condition forces nilpotence
explanation: Efim Zelmanov proved a major restricted form of the Burnside problem for Lie algebras, showing that certain identities and local nilpotence conditions force the whole algebra to be nilpotent. Nilpotent here means that sufficiently long repeated combinations eventually vanish.
whyItMatters: The work introduced techniques that Zelmanov later used to solve the restricted Burnside problem for groups.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1988
title: Euler's fourth-power conjecture falls
explanation: Noam Elkies found a counterexample to Euler's conjecture for fourth powers: three positive fourth powers can add to a fourth power. Roger Frye then used a computer search to find the smallest such counterexample later that year.
whyItMatters: The result combined theoretical insight with computation and showed again that plausible generalizations of Fermat's equation can fail.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1989
title: A Banach-space problem is settled
explanation: Jean Bourgain solved the long-standing Lp problem about special arrangements of vectors in function spaces, using both analytic and probabilistic ideas. These infinite-dimensional spaces extend familiar ideas about distance and coordinates far beyond ordinary geometry.
whyItMatters: The proof demonstrated how probability can uncover structure in analysis and advanced the geometry of Banach spaces.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1980-1990 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1990
title: Quantum groups reshape symmetry
explanation: Vladimir Drinfeld received a Fields Medal for work including quantum groups, algebraic structures that deform familiar symmetry groups using an extra parameter. Despite their name, they are mathematical objects with important connections to quantum physics rather than groups in the ordinary technical sense.
whyItMatters: Quantum groups linked algebra, topology, solvable physical models and knot invariants in an unexpectedly unified way.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1990-2000 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1991
title: The restricted Burnside problem is solved
explanation: Efim Zelmanov proved that, for fixed numbers of generators and a fixed exponent, only finitely many finite groups of that type are possible. This solved the restricted Burnside problem; it is distinct from the original Burnside question, whose answer can be negative.
whyItMatters: The proof brought together deep ideas from group theory and Lie algebras and completed a program that had lasted much of the twentieth century.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1990-2000 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1992
title: A matrix integral proves Witten's conjecture
explanation: Maxim Kontsevich proved Witten's conjecture connecting intersection numbers on moduli spaces of curves with the KdV differential equation. His proof encoded the geometry using graphs and a special integral over matrices called the matrix Airy function.
whyItMatters: The result built a precise bridge among geometry, combinatorics, differential equations and ideas from quantum gravity.
sourceTitle: Intersection Theory on the Moduli Space of Curves and the Matrix Airy Function

label: A mathematical story from 1993
title: Alternating knot diagrams are connected by flypes
explanation: Menasco and Thistlethwaite proved Tait's flyping conjecture: any two reduced alternating diagrams of the same prime knot are related by a sequence of simple moves called flypes. A flype rotates part of a knot diagram while preserving the knot itself.
whyItMatters: The theorem completed the classical Tait conjectures and gave knot theorists strong control over alternating diagrams.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1990-2000 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1994
title: Fermat's Last Theorem is proved
people: Andrew Wiles, with a crucial final step completed with Richard Taylor
explanation: After a gap was found in his 1993 announcement, Andrew Wiles and Richard Taylor repaired the argument in 1994. Their work proved enough of the modularity conjecture to establish that no positive integers satisfy x^n + y^n = z^n when n is greater than 2.
whyItMatters: The proof closed a 350-year-old problem and united elliptic curves, modular forms and Galois representations.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1990-2000 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1995
title: A formula jumps directly to distant digits of pi
people: Simon Plouffe, David Bailey and Peter Borwein
explanation: Simon Plouffe discovered the BBP formula in 1995, and Bailey, Borwein and Plouffe later published it in 1997. The formula can calculate a hexadecimal or binary digit of pi far along its expansion without first calculating every earlier digit.
whyItMatters: It revealed an unexpected structure in pi and created new ways to test huge computations and search for digit-extraction formulas.
sourceTitle: On the Rapid Computation of Various Polylogarithmic Constants - Mathematics of Computation

label: A mathematical story from 1996
title: Lattice cryptography gains a worst-case foundation
explanation: Miklós Ajtai showed how to generate random lattice problems whose average-case difficulty is connected to the worst-case difficulty of fundamental lattice problems. This was a new kind of security foundation: breaking typical generated instances would also solve every instance of a related hard problem.
whyItMatters: The result began the modern theory of lattice-based cryptography, now important for constructing systems designed to resist quantum attacks.
sourceTitle: Generating Hard Instances of Lattice Problems - IBM Research

label: A mathematical story from 1997
title: A theorem prover resolves the Robbins problem
people: William McCune and the EQP theorem prover
explanation: William McCune published the solution found by his EQP program showing that every Robbins algebra is a Boolean algebra. The computer produced a valid chain of algebraic deductions for a question that had remained open since the 1930s.
whyItMatters: The proof became a landmark example of automated reasoning solving a recognized mathematical problem rather than merely checking a human proof.
sourceTitle: Robbins Algebras Are Boolean - William McCune, University of New Mexico

label: A mathematical story from 1998
title: Kepler's sphere-packing conjecture is proved
people: Thomas Hales, with extensive computations and contributions from Samuel Ferguson
explanation: Thomas Hales announced a proof that the familiar grocer's arrangement is the densest possible packing of equal spheres in three-dimensional space. The argument combined traditional mathematics with large computer checks, and its exceptionally difficult verification later motivated a fully formal proof project.
whyItMatters: The result settled a problem posed by Kepler in 1611 and advanced methods for computer-assisted and formally verified mathematics.
sourceTitle: Chronology for 1990-2000 - MacTutor History of Mathematics

label: A mathematical story from 1999
title: All rational elliptic curves become modular
people: Christophe Breuil, Brian Conrad, Fred Diamond and Richard Taylor
explanation: Work completed in 1999 by Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor extended modularity from the semistable elliptic curves handled in Wiles's proof to every elliptic curve over the rational numbers. Their papers established the full theorem that the earlier Taniyama-Shimura-Weil conjecture predicted.
whyItMatters: The modularity theorem gives a powerful translation between equations defining elliptic curves and analytic modular forms.
sourceTitle: On the Modularity of Elliptic Curves over Q - Journal of the American Mathematical Society
